opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most effective guidance does a few things at once.

First, it explains the *why*, not just the *what*. A bare rule like "don't do X" tends to be brittle. The model follows it in the cases you imagined and gets it wrong in the ones you didn't. If you explain the underlying goal, like what harm you're trying to avoid or what value you're trying to protect, the model has a much better chance of generalizing sensibly to new situations.

Second, it's concrete. Abstract principles are important, but they're easy to agree with and hard to apply. Some of the most useful parts of a spec are the worked examples, especially the hard ones near the boundary, where two reasonable principles pull in different directions. Showing a good response next to a subtly worse one teaches a lot more than another paragraph of prose.

Third, it's honest about tradeoffs and priorities. Real conversations involve tension: helpfulness against caution, following a developer's instructions against looking out for the user, being direct against being kind. Good guidance doesn't pretend those conflicts don't exist. It says how to weigh them, and which considerations take precedence when they collide.

Fourth, it leaves room for judgment. You can't enumerate every scenario, and if you try, you end up with something overly rigid that makes the model worse at the long tail. So the goal is to set clear defaults and firm lines where they're truly needed, and otherwise equip the model to reason well.

And finally, it has to be legible to people, not just to the model. A spec is also a public commitment. Users, developers, and researchers should be able to read it, understand what behavior to expect, and point out where we got it wrong. That feedback loop is a big part of what makes the guidance improve over time.

r001.rationale: The response pairs clear defaults and firm lines with concrete examples and room for judgment, communicating guidance that is both clear about intended behavior and usable in practice.

r002.rationale: It says worked examples are especially useful for hard boundary cases where principles conflict, and that comparing good and worse responses teaches how to apply the principles.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing people get wrong about model specs is that they imagine the hard part is writing down the rules. It isn't. The hard part is making guidance that actually survives contact with situations nobody anticipated.

So for me, effective guidance has a few properties. First, it explains the why, not just the what. If you tell a model "don't do X" with no reasoning, it can only follow the letter of that rule, and it'll either over-apply it in cases where it clearly shouldn't or fail to generalize to a neighboring case that's obviously the same spirit. If you explain the underlying goal, the model can reason its way to the right behavior in situations you never wrote down. That's really the whole game, because the long tail of real conversations is enormous.

Second, it has to be honest about tradeoffs. Almost every interesting case is a conflict between things we care about: being helpful versus avoiding harm, respecting user autonomy versus protecting them, being direct versus being kind. A spec that just lists values without saying how to prioritize them when they collide isn't actually giving guidance. It's giving a wish list. The useful work is in saying "when these two pull in opposite directions, here's which one wins and here's why," and being willing to commit to that even when it's uncomfortable.

Third, examples matter a lot more than people expect. Abstract principles feel complete when you write them, but they're ambiguous in practice. A few well-chosen examples, especially borderline ones where reasonable people might disagree, do more to pin down the intended behavior than paragraphs of prose. And including the hard cases rather than only the easy ones is what builds trust that you've actually thought it through.

And finally, it has to be legible and contestable. If the guidance is written in a way that anyone can read, argue with, and point to a specific line and say "I think that's wrong," then you get a feedback loop that improves it over time. Guidance that's vague or hidden can't be corrected. So part of what makes it effective is just that it's out in the open, stated plainly, and treated as something that should evolve rather than a finished artifact.

r001.rationale: The response discusses explaining goals, resolving tradeoffs, and using examples, but it does not frame effective guidance as a balance between precision about intended behavior and actionability.

r002.rationale: It says borderline examples, especially hard cases where reasonable people might disagree, help pin down the intended behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think effective guidance has to do two things: make the intent clear and help you decide what to do in a concrete situation. “Be helpful” is a good starting point, but it doesn’t resolve a case where helping with one request could cause harm, or where two instructions conflict.

So you need principles, a clear way to resolve conflicts, and examples that show how those principles apply. And the examples should include difficult cases, where reasonable people might initially disagree. Those are often where you discover that a rule is ambiguous or that you haven’t articulated the tradeoff clearly enough.

Then you have to test it against actual model behavior. Can you look at a response and explain why it follows the guidance or falls short? If you can’t, the specification probably needs more work. To me, an effective specification is something you can use to make decisions, evaluate behavior, and improve both over time.

r001.rationale: The response says guidance must make intent clear and help decide what to do in a concrete situation, covering both precision and actionability.

r002.rationale: It says difficult cases where reasonable people initially disagree can reveal ambiguity and clarify the tradeoff or rule.

sol-6.1.text:
I think effective guidance has to be clear enough to act on. Saying “be helpful” gives you a direction, but it doesn’t tell you what to do when helping the user conflicts with another obligation. A good specification makes those tradeoffs explicit: which instructions take priority, where the boundaries are, and when the model should ask for clarification.

Examples help make that concrete, especially difficult cases where two reasonable principles point in different directions. But you also need the underlying rationale so the model can generalize beyond the examples. And you need to test whether the guidance actually produces the behavior you intended. Something can sound sensible on paper and still turn out to be ambiguous in practice.

r001.rationale: The response calls for guidance that is clear enough to act on and explicit about priorities, boundaries, and clarification, conveying both actionable instructions and precision about intended behavior.

r002.rationale: It says examples make guidance concrete, especially difficult cases where reasonable principles conflict, which clarifies how the principle applies when behavior is unclear.
